name: Pfafflar
kurzbeschreibung: Secluded, rustic village nestled in the remote Namlostal valley, offering the most authentic Tiroler nature.
beschreibung:
Overview

Pfafflar is nestled in the wild and romantic Bschlabertal, a steep tributary valley branching off the Tyrolean Lech Valley within the Lechtal Alps in the district of Reutte. This alpine mountain municipality consists of three sunny hamlets: Bschlabs (1,314 m) at the valley entrance, Boden (1,356 m) at the valley head, and the historic alpine hamlet of Pfafflar (approx. 1,500 m) along the switchbacks of the Hahntennjoch road. Covering 33.6 square kilometres with only around 100 permanent residents, Pfafflar is by far the smallest municipality in the district of Reutte and one of the most sparsely populated in all of Austria. Visitors experience genuine Mountaineering Village character, profound silence, and pristine high-alpine beauty far from tourist commercialization. Flanked north and south by the jagged ridges of the Lechtal Alps, the breathtaking scenic high-mountain road over the Hahntennjoch pass (1,894 m) links the valley in summer directly with Imst in the Inn Valley.

History

Settlement of this secluded high valley began around 1280 under the initiative of the Lords of Starkenberg, settled by pastoralists arriving across the mountains from the Inn Valley. The settlement was first documented in 1284 under the Rhaeto-Romanic names Pavelaers (fodder barn or pasture) and Bislafes (behind the waters). Pfafflar was originally one of the highest permanently inhabited year-round settlements in Tyrol at over 1,500 metres. However, because winters were exceptionally snow-heavy and threatened by avalanches, the inhabitants abandoned permanent year-round habitation in 1894, relocating their primary homes to the lower hamlets of Boden and Bschlabs; since then, the hamlet of Pfafflar has functioned exclusively as a summer pasture settlement. Its listed log-timber chalets date partly to the 13th century and were constructed entirely without iron nails – a unique architectural treasure. Historically linked to Imst across the pass, the municipality became part of Reutte in 1938. In Bschlabs stands the Baroque pilgrimage church Maria Schnee (1640).

Getting There

Access to Pfafflar depends greatly on the alpine seasons. During summer (typically June to October), the Hahntennjoch provincial road L246 is open from both directions: either climbing from Imst in the Inn Valley over the 1,894-metre Hahntennjoch pass or ascending from Elmen in the Lech Valley. In winter, the Hahntennjoch pass is strictly closed due to avalanche danger; the villages of Bschlabs and Boden are then accessible exclusively from the Lech Valley via Elmen on the well-maintained L246. Rail passengers arrive at Reutte in Tirol station on the Außerfern Railway, or in summer via Imst-Pitztal station. The VVT valley bus route 4268 connects Elmen to Bschlabs and Boden, offering direct transfers to the main Lech Valley bus line 110.

Tips

A journey into the past awaits in the protected alpine village of Pfafflar, with its sun-blackened timber chalets operating rustic summer snack taverns. A unique cultural highlight is the Path of the Senses (Weg der Sinne) in Bschlabs: this seven-kilometre circular trail leads from the pilgrimage church Maria Schnee across a suspended wooden footbridge over the wild Bschlaber Klamm gorge, decorated along the path with expressive wooden sculptures and contemplative quotes. The mountaineering hamlet of Boden serves as the premier gateway for alpine summit ascents: from here, hikers follow the classic path up to the historic Hanauer Hütte (1,922 m) beneath the Dremelspitze peak, renowned for challenging via ferratas. In winter, the deep snows of the valley attract ski tourers and snowshoers seeking profound alpine solitude.
